src/fan.ts: worktrees, probes, guards, promote, resume, clean. Each probe returns {i, ok, score, diffstat, summary, worktree, tokens, wall_s, exit_code, timed_out, log_path, truncated, error}. `ok` describes the PROCESS and `score` the CANDIDATE — a probe can finish cleanly and fail f, and a probe whose agent crashed can still leave a passing tree, so both are measured and reported separately. `best` names the highest-scoring probe that PASSED f; a failing probe with a spectacular number is not a winner

the four guards from pi-subagent's pattern, because a probe is itself an agent that can call avo fan: depth (AVO_FAN_DEPTH default 3, counted by AVO_FAN_LEVEL), cycles (AVO_FAN_CHAIN of prompt hashes), concurrency min(8,cpus-2) reusing score.ts's mapLimit rather than a second one, and a 900s default timeout whose kill takes the whole process group. The state travels in the environment because that is the only channel that survives spawn into an arbitrary agent binary. A guard is a REFUSAL (exit 1), not a harness error — the same shape avo commit uses when it declines a candidate

--promote <i> applies one probe's diff to the root working tree and STOPS: it does not score, does not commit, does not delete the other probes. avo commit is the only writer of a version (invariant 1) and promotion is the explicit separate step invariant 7 asks for. The patch is written to .avo/worktrees/<run>/promote-<i>.patch BEFORE it is applied, so a rejected promotion still leaves something to inspect; --3way is a fallback used only when the plain apply fails, and it says so

crash safety: the manifest is rewritten after EVERY probe, not at the end, so a kill leaves the finished work recoverable. --resume re-runs only the probes that never finished, re-creating a worktree the kill destroyed, and re-checks the guards because a resume spawns agents too. --list and --clean <id|all> were added beyond the planned surface: cleanup removes UNTOUCHED worktrees by design (a changed one is the only copy of that work), so without an explicit cleaner `git worktree list` fills up

stall = N attempts since the last committed improvement. P_t is monotone, so the newest version IS the last improvement — an attempt that PASSED f and still did not beat it counts, because it did not move P_t. That is the distinction that makes the signal mean 'not progressing' rather than 'failing'

thrash = K consecutive attempts that failed the same way. The signature is the harness errors when there are any, else the scorer's own first log line, with temp dirs, shas and numbers folded to placeholders (hex BEFORE digits, or a sha would be partly digested into N first and two runs of the same broken code would stop matching)

the directive CITES: prior versions with their scores and rationales, the dead ends memory holds, and the docs in K that no version has ever mentioned — the last list computed by matching each doc's title against every --why and every memory, so a doc appears precisely because nothing in the lineage talks about it. 'Try something else' is worthless; the agent already believes it is trying something else. This is what S3 and S4 were for: without a lineage and a knowledge base there is nothing concrete to cite

a thrash directive says something DIFFERENT from a stall directive — read the failure, get back to a measurable state, change direction not degree — because telling a thrashing agent to explore K is telling it to do more of what is already failing

fixed a real bug the new e2e caught by failing INTERMITTENTLY: which attempts count as 'since the best version' is decided by the sha each attempt recorded, not by its clock. An attempt scored on top of v3 carries v3's sha; the attempt that BECAME v3 was scored before that commit existed and carries its parent's. Time cannot separate them — git truncates author dates to the second, so the committing attempt's millisecond ts can read as LATER than the commit it produced and the stall fires one early forever. Flooring to the second (the first fix) then made a fast scorer's attempts vanish into the commit's own second instead. The clock stays as the fallback for an attempt whose head matches neither (the agent made its own commits), with a full second of margin

the turn prompt is the only continuity there is, and that is the thing most easily got wrong: every iteration is a FRESH PROCESS with no memory of the last one. Iteration 1 gets the operator's prompt verbatim; every later one gets it plus what the previous iteration decided plus the state, plus the directive when one fired. PLAN's item (1), the iteration log: ensureTrajectoryIgnored is now ADDITIVE rather than write-once. It returned early whenever .avo/.gitignore existed, so .avo/runs/ would have been ignored only in repos created after this slice — the worst kind of divergence, the kind that works on the machine that added it. A file carrying our marker (matched by the `# written by avo` PREFIX, so files written before `avo run` existed still qualify) gains the entries it is missing; a file without the marker is the operator's and is never touched. An insight is injected at prime time, so every future session would open with a stale 'you are stalling, read v3' from a run that ended days ago. avo mem lists interventions; avo mem prime does not. It cannot be a lineage commit either — invariant 1 says avo commit is the only writer of a version, and an intervention is not one

PLAN's item (3), crash safety: the manifest IS the --json report. PLAN's item (4), guards: the same four as avo fan, on the SAME budget (AVO_FAN_DEPTH/LEVEL/CHAIN) rather than a second set. A turn is an agent that can call avo run, and a loop inside a loop is the same exponential hazard as a fan-out inside one; two separate budgets would each permit three levels. A guard is a refusal (exit 1), not a harness error

four stop conditions, each for a reason: --max-iters (the budget is the operator's); .avo/STOP (the one command meant to run for days needs a brake that does not require finding the process, and one an AGENT can reach when the task is genuinely done); MAX_CONSECUTIVE_NOOPS=3 (an unchanged tree is never scored, so it records no attempt and the supervisor CANNOT see it — the one stop condition steering cannot express); and an agent binary that cannot be started (it will not start on the next iteration either, and retrying it nine more times is precisely the spinning the rules forbid)

a no-op only counts as one when HEAD did not move. An agent that ran avo commit itself leaves a clean tree, and calling that 'nothing happened' would stop a loop that is working. head_before/head_after are recorded per iteration for exactly this

task: ralph: an interrupted loop takes its session with it
done: Started this cycle by orienting and found 2,279 lines of uncommitted S8 work in the tree. Read it, ran the health check green, and then watched `git diff HEAD` go to EMPTY between two adjacent tool calls: files read as untracked came back tracked-and-unmodified, and a commit nobody in this session made (0739e17) appeared on the branch. The tree was being rewritten underneath me.

Diagnosed it from the process table rather than guessing. PID 151851, a `claude --print` session started 11:46:13, cwd this repo, whose `timeout` parent had been reparented to `systemd --user` (PID 3420, parent 1) — its `ralph.sh` was GONE. The operator then started `./ralph.sh 45` at 11:59:52, which spawned me. Two agent sessions, one working tree. The orphan committed S8, opened PR #31 and merged it while I was mid-orientation, and my `just e2e` ran against a tree it was rewriting.

The cause is in ralph.sh and the fix was already sitting uncommitted in the tree from a previous cycle: the session ran as a FOREGROUND PIPELINE, and bash defers trap handlers until the running foreground command returns, so Ctrl+C was not acted on until the session ended on its own — minutes, for an agent turn. Worse, when the loop finally left, nothing signalled the session at all, so it survived, reparented, still editing.

Shipped that fix (PR #34, merged fb69ad3): the session runs as an async job so `wait` is interruptible and the handler runs the instant the signal lands; the whole process tree is LISTED before anything is signalled, because killing a parent reparents its survivors and loses the trail to them; signalled pid by pid rather than by process group, because `timeout` puts itself in a group of its own and `kill -- -$pgid` would miss the session underneath it; TERM escalated to KILL after 3s; and the between-iteration breather made interruptible too, so Ctrl+C in the backoff is not held until the backoff expires. Exit 130 and a `stopped on interrupt` summary, so an interrupted iteration is not counted a failure.

task: S8b (pi): the supervisor extension — one stall, one directive
done: Shipped pi/extensions/avo-supervisor/{index.ts,supervisor.ts} (PR #36, merged d4e6991): subscribes to tool_result, and on avo_score or avo_commit calls the same supervise() the CLI calls and injects S7's directive with pi.sendMessage. A SECOND extension, not a second half of the first — the tools are useful without steering, and an operator already running `avo run` wants that pairing. `avo install --agent pi` links both.

The design question the slice turned on: what is the UNIT of steering. Answered EPISODE, not attempt. episodeKeys() names the run of consecutive readings that are the same problem — a stall by the best version it is stuck under plus the attempt index it began at, a thrash by its failure signature plus where the streak began — and one episode gets one directive. Re-injecting the same advice every attempt burns context and teaches the model to skim the one message meant to change its mind. A NEW best, or a thrash appearing during a stall, is new information and does steer. The key is a pure function of the supervision state, which is what keeps it from needing a counter that could drift from the CLI's.

The bug that would have shipped silently: the episode anchor must be `analyzed - since_best`, NOT `attempts - since_best`. Past ANALYSIS_WINDOW (1000) the detector sees only a window, so the untruncated total creeps up once per attempt while the window's own numbers hold still — the key would change every attempt and re-steer forever, in exactly the long-running loop the supervisor exists for. Caught by reasoning about the saturated case rather than by a failure, and there is now a test at that boundary.

Branching: Pi's docs say to persist extension state in tool-result `details`, and that is wrong for this extension — it owns no tool, and a tool_result handler that returned `details` would CLOBBER the avo tool's own (ToolResultEventResult.details replaces). The injected custom_message already carries the episodes and is already branch-scoped, so session_start reconstructs from ctx.sessionManager.getBranch() — never getEntries(), because entries off the branch belong to a path the model no longer remembers and treating them as answered leaves a real stall unsteered. Tested three ways: same branch does not re-steer, a branch that never saw the directive does.

Kept iter 10's decision rather than re-opening it: state comes from .avo/attempts.jsonl and the git lineage through supervise() every time, with thresholds left null so .avo/config.json decides exactly as it does for the CLI. A test proves it steers on a stall that happened entirely BEFORE the session existed. Every steer is also an intervention memory keyed by the episode, so a Pi trajectory audits like an `avo run` one and re-recording is idempotent (invariant 5). Nothing re-implements the commit rule, the thresholds or the directive text (invariant 1).

The SDK-driven acceptance is test/pi-supervise-drive.ts, and what it scripts is the MODEL, not the harness: real DefaultResourceLoader, real ExtensionRunner (bindCore/setUIContext/emitToolResult), real SessionManager.inMemory(), with tool calls executed through the definitions Pi registered. A stalling sequence driven by an actual LLM is neither deterministic nor offline, and the thing under test reacts to tool results rather than to prose. What it buys over the unit suite is the two things unit tests cannot reach: Pi routing a CUSTOM tool's result to a handler in a DIFFERENT extension, and pi.sendMessage from inside that handler reaching the session.

MATMUL WAS THE FIRST CANDIDATE AND LOST ON MEASUREMENT, before any of the above was written. Its own repo, never this one, and enforced rather than documented: avo commit writes Avo-Version commits into the repo it is pointed at, so a target inside this checkout would put the loop's entire lineage into avocode's history AND score a tree the loop is also editing — the S3/S6/S8 self-perturbation bug in its worst form. init.sh resolves the destination to an absolute path and refuses anything under $root; a check asserts it wrote nothing there.

correct is THREE gates, not one. (1) the protected files hash to what init.sh recorded in .avo/gate.sha256, (2) node --test passes, (3) bench/run.js re-checks the candidate against the independent reference ON THE EXACT INPUT IT IS ABOUT TO BE TIMED ON, and that it did not mutate its arguments. Gate 3 costs the naive reference on every score (~0.7s) and it is the one that earns it: the suite ships a candidate that passes the ENTIRE unit suite and returns [] for any corpus over 1000 words. Only gate 3 sees it. templates/score/README.md's own rule — keep the correctness check independent of the code under optimization — is unenforceable without a full-scale check.

The hash gate is deliberately NOT oversold. It covers .avo/score itself, but an agent editing both the scorer and the hash file defeats it from inside; bench/init.sh --verify is the external audit that cannot be reached from the target repo. Sample counts are adaptive and spread_pct is an INTERQUARTILE RANGE, not max-min. A 385x ladder makes any fixed rep count wrong at one end. minReps 3 / maxReps 500 / budgetMs 300 gives the 556ms baseline 3 samples and the 0.9ms candidate 469. The first version used max-min and reported 51% 'spread' at the fast end — one GC pause, a statistic that GROWS with the sample count, i.e. reading as noisier precisely because the measurement got better. On the IQR every step is 0-2.5% here and 1.3% worst on the runner, which is what makes floor 0.03 a measurement rather than a guess. A check asserts the worst measured spread is under the configured floor, so the two cannot drift apart silently.

Two bugs found by writing the thing that would catch them.
